title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids
text: BASS objective: The two main objectives for BASS are to: 1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible). 2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.

title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids
text: BASS hypothesis: BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.

title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids
text: BASS approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction. This investigation explored two primary air flow configurations; concurrent-flow and opposed-flow. With concurrent-flow air flows in the same direction as the flame spread and in opposed-flow air flows in the opposite direction of flame spread.

title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids
text: BASS approach: Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching. The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric. Other sample shapes were utilized as well including spheres and cylinders.

title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids
text: BASS research impacts: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques. BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity.

title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids
text: BASS research impacts: Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

title: BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
text: BASS-II hypothesis: BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature, etc.). NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed. We are interested in finding the fundamental limit for a given material.

title: BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
text: BASS-II approach: To summarize, BASS-II's approach, microgravity combustion tests were performed aboard the International Space Station. Active crew support for real-time “lab partner” operations. The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment. Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen). Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.

title: BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
text: BASS-II research impacts: A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you’re on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning. These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems.

title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: FLEX objective: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations.

title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: FLEX objective: These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.

title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: FLEX hypothesis: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.

title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: FLEX approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI. The basic outline of the procedure to construct this diagram is as follows: 1. Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests. 2. Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm) 3. Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion (as opposed to extinguishing at a finite droplet size). 4. Perform a droplet combustion test. 5. Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed). 6.

title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: FLEX approach: Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction). 7. Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction. 8. Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite. There were ambient conditions where the extinction droplet sizes at all ambient oxygen mole fractions were too small to either be observed or measured with the available diagnostics. In this case, the determination of the LOI is similar, but more iterative. Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI.

title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: FLEX approach: For the slow flow tests (in the flight experiment), the configuration of the flight hardware did not allow for adequate diagnostics over the entire test for a droplet in a uniform, steady convective flow. In these tests, the procedure will be to duplicate tests above which yield finite-sized extinction droplet diameters. Near the end of the tests, prior to flame extinction, the droplet will be subjected to a small, sub-buoyant, convective flow (imparted by translating the droplet at a slow, uniform speed). The goal of the experiment is then to see how the presence of this flow influences the extinction process. Note, a large number of the tests involve free droplets (as opposed to fiber-supported droplets) and a number of these tests will have droplets with a slow drift velocity.

title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: FLEX approach: Data gathered from these tests to examine the influences of a small, sub-buoyant flow on both the burning and extinction process.

title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: FLEX research impacts: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events.

title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment
text: FLEX research impacts: Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications. Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.

title: SAFFIRE-I — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
text: SAFFIRE-I objective: The objectives of this investigation were to: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.

title: SAFFIRE-I — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
text: SAFFIRE-I hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.

title: SAFFIRE-I — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
text: SAFFIRE-I approach: The Saffire-1 experiments was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras.

title: SAFFIRE-I — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
text: SAFFIRE-I approach: In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked.

title: SAFFIRE-I — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
text: SAFFIRE-I research impacts: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

title: SAFFIRE-III — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III
text: SAFFIRE-III objective: The objectives of this investigation were to: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.

title: SAFFIRE-III — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III
text: SAFFIRE-III hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.

title: SAFFIRE-III — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III
text: SAFFIRE-III approach: The Saffire-III experiments were performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire 1 investigation, the Saffire III investigation also used SIBAL as the sample material. However, the experiments were conducted at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s compared to 20 cm/s during Saffire I. The flow was either concurrent or opposed. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.

title: SAFFIRE-III — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III
text: SAFFIRE-III research impacts: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

title: SAME — Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
text: SAME objective: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.

title: SAME — Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
text: SAME hypothesis: The three hypotheses that motivated this investigation: In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke).

title: SAME — Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
text: SAME hypothesis: The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.

title: SAME — Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
text: SAME approach: The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds), and initiated the thermophoretic soot samplers to sample the smoke. The actual duration of each combustion event was typically 2 minutes. After flight, the particulate collected on the thermophoretic probes were analyzed using a Transmission Electron microscope (TEM) to determine primary and aggregate particle dimensions. The remains of the samples were weighed to determine their mass loss. The digital data was transcribed from the video record and analyzed to determine the response of the detectors.

title: SAME — Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
text: SAME approach: Once the flight mass loss rates were determined, 1-g operation conditions to produce the same loss were determined.The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials where variables such as the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.

title: SAME — Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
text: SAME research impacts: The SAME experiment will provide technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated.The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories.

title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
text: ACME BRE objective: The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows. 1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. 2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.

title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
text: ACME BRE hypothesis: The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties. Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible. The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment. It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point. This could enable the Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) test as a basis for establishing flammability maps for real materials.

title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
text: ACME BRE hypothesis: The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before.

title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
text: ACME BRE approach: To accomplish the above objectives, flight experiments are proposed. Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests. For each test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure. Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition. The flames will initially be observed without varying the fuel flow rate. Because burner surface temperature and heat flux will vary, this will allow a broad range of conditions to be observed during a single test. As the surface temperature of the burner increases, and the flame remains steady, a continuous set of data is produced for the flammability map.

title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
text: ACME BRE approach: Eventually either the flame will extinguish, the surface temperature of the burner will equilibrate, or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor will be reached. At this time the fuel flow will be terminated. So a test should terminate for a given flow rate at extinction, and for continued burning when the burner surface temperature has steadied or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor is neared. The extinction limit could be found once the burner temperature has steadied, and the heat flux sensor has not exceeded its limit. At that state, the flow rate can be reduced in small increments, until extinction is observed and the flow rate shut off. Again, in this process, new data is being produced for the flammability map. Ignition limit tests are not proposed for microgravity, but we will explore these under normal gravity.

title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
text: ACME BRE approach: We believe there is better control on Earth-based ignition testing and that these results should carry over to microgravity conditions. In addition to the flight experiments, in normal gravity testing will continue. These tests will involve gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels. These experiments will further establish the validation of the BRE for 1-g applications and show its usefulness to establish 1-g ignition and extinction limits. As available, drop facility testing will be used to refine procedures, test instrumentation, and help to establish viable flow conditions. We will also pursue a CFD model for the quiescent microgravity burning. This will also guide us in the flight experiments, and potentially provide a predictive methodology.

title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
text: ACME BRE research impacts: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

text: ACME CFI-G objective: 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS). 2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. title: ACME CFI-G — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
text: ACME CFI-G hypothesis: The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.

text: ACME CFI-G approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.

title: ACME CFI-G — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
text: ACME CFI-G research impacts: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

title: ACME E-FIELD — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
text: ACME E-FIELD approach: The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces. The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. In the former case, the tests are conducted using the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment. An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. Measurements, as a function of the field strength and fuel, are taken of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing.

title: ACME E-FIELD — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
text: ACME E-FIELD approach: The gas-jet burner is used to create a small, focused flame for detailed ion-driven convection studies while the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow to enable flame stability and soot behavior analysis. A high-voltage copper mesh electrode positioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength. The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior. Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength. Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames. Voltage-current curves were recorded to assess the relationship between electric field strength and chemi-ion current, revealing ion-driven convection effects.

title: ACME E-FIELD — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
text: ACME E-FIELD approach: High-resolution cameras captured flame shape, luminosity, and soot distribution. Spectral imaging with filters measures chemiluminescent emissions and soot volume fraction. There were thermopile detectors to measure flame radiant emissions. All experiments were conducted in the combustion integrated rack (CIR). Tests were administered with Glenn Research Center (GRC) directing astronaut actions. Parameters such as fuel flow rate, coflow velocity, and field polarity are were varied to isolate specific effects on ion production, flame stability, and soot behavior.

title: ACME E-FIELD — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
text: ACME E-FIELD research impacts: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

title: DAFT — Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2
text: DAFT objective: The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak, to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process. DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity. Summarized objectives include: 1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity 2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control 3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity 4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments.

title: DAFT — Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2
text: DAFT hypothesis: The TSI P-Trak operates by condensing isopropanol around aerosol particulates that are subsequently laser counted. It was hypothesized that the P-Trak would not work in microgravity due to two potential failure modes that exist. 1) the system would clog or become obscured by isopropanol, and 2) the internal air-flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device will cause an over counting of particulates. The TSI P-Trak was modified for microgravity use via using capillary action to recycle the isopropanol. Therefore, there are two basic hypotheses: 1) that the P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity. 2) that the aerosol created and filtered per the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices.

title: DAFT — Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2
text: DAFT approach: The experimental approach consists of the following components: 1) Modification of Instrumentation: TSI P-Trak was modified for use in microgravity by redesigning the condenser tube to use capillary forces for recycling isopropyl alcohol and removing the mercury switch responsible for detecting instrument orientation. 2) Aerosol Generation: Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard due to its ease of dispersion. The ARD was aerosolized with GN2 to create particle samples. The aerosol was contained within 15-liter Mylar bags. 3) On-Orbit Testing: The modified P-Trak gathered data from counting aerosol particles and these data were compared to the DustTrak CNC specifically designed to work in microgravity.

title: ACME CLD — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
text: ACME CLD approach: ACME CLD Flame project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot sub-models that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high soot loading levels. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be important for achieving both goals. Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions. For the more dilute flames, measurements will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height and flame shape as extinction limits are approached. The sooting tendencies of the more fuel-rich flames will be investigated using soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements to determine soot temperatures and soot volume fractions.

title: ACME CLD — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
text: ACME CLD approach: Flame temperatures in non-sooting regions will be measured using thin-filament pyrometry. Based on observations, modifications can be made to the kinetics and soot model to match better the experimental results. If the overall agreement of the measurements and computations is good, the results of the computations can be “mined” to provide insight on species (and hence chemical processes) that cannot be measured directly using the diagnostics available for the proposed experiment.

title: ACME CLD — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
text: ACME CLD research impacts: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place. In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency. While normal gravity combustion studies can provide important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces often complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results. Momentum effects dominate most practical combustion devices, but the contribution of buoyancy forces is hard to eliminate in normal gravity.

text: ACME s-Flame approach: A series of experiments is proposed in which mixtures of various gaseous fuels and diluents will be issued into an oxidizing environment through a spherical porous burner and ignited to obtain, nominally, a spherical, one-dimensional stabilized flame. Synchronized measurements are to be made including spectrally resolved images, flame and burner temperatures, radiative flux measurements, and system operating conditions (including reactant flow rates, ambient temperatures, pressures and acceleration levels, etc.). These data are to be used for comparisons of flame behavior and structure with detailed numerical simulations of the flames. Conventional gaseous fuels including hydrogen, methane, and ethylene will be used. Hydrogen is the simplest fuel and its reaction mechanism is also reasonably established.

title: BASS-Modeling — Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
text: BASS-Modeling objective: The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways. To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds.

title: BASS-Modeling — Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
text: BASS-Modeling objective: The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.

title: BASS-Modeling — Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
text: BASS-Modeling hypothesis: The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was believed to be able to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including phenomena such as the “Goldilocks” flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport, and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics.

title: BASS-Modeling — Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
text: BASS-Modeling approach: The approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation to study concurrent flame spread in microgravity. A previously developed computational framework was employed to run fully coupled simulations of fluid–solid responses, focusing on materials subject to charring and ablation. Within this framework, the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders. Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions.

title: BASS-Modeling — Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
text: BASS-Modeling approach: The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the “Goldilocks” flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions.

title: BASS-Modeling — Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
text: BASS-Modeling research impacts: This research provides predictive tools for screening new materials’ flammability limits, which can lead to the design of safer spacecrafts. The development of Large Eddy Simulation subgrid models is expected to improve hazard assessment capabilities critical for managing fire risks during long-duration space missions and within confined spacecraft habitats. On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards. The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies and foster innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios.

title: CFI — Cool Flames Investigation
text: CFI objective: The objectives of this investigation are to: 1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm. 2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior. 3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics. 4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.

title: CFI — Cool Flames Investigation
text: CFI hypothesis: Flame combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels such as n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and faresane in microgravity can provide insights into low-temperature chemical kinetics, revealing critical parameters like droplet extinction diameters and flame dynamics that are not observable on Earth.

title: CFI — Cool Flames Investigation
text: CFI approach: The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) contains the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) which facilitates the controlled combustion of fuel droplets. A system of gas bottles and fuel syringes delivers the desired gas mixture to the combustion chamber ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 atm. Droplets of fuel are dispensed and suspended between hypodermic needles or tethered using silicon-carbide fibers. A hot-wire igniter is positioned near the droplet for ignition. After ignition the wire is retracted. Fuels observed include n-dodecane, farnesane, and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane. Fuels diluted with molecular oxygen, atomic nitrogen, and helium to study the influence on flame extinction and dynamics. title: Cool-flame CFD — Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
text: Cool-flame CFD objective: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.

title: Cool-flame CFD — Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
text: Cool-flame CFD hypothesis: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.

title: Cool-flame CFD — Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
text: Cool-flame CFD approach: OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets. To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure.

title: Fire aboard space station Mir, 1997 (NASA History)
text: Listed by the challenge: a multinational crew survived a fire aboard Mir caused by an oxygen generator failure.

title: Moon base atmosphere (challenge text)
text: The challenge states that the Moon base and pressurized rovers are expected to use an oxygen concentration of 30% or greater at a pressure of 10.2 psi (70.3 kPa) or less, between a spacesuit (100% O2 at 4.3 psi) and Earth air, which makes materials more flammable.

title: Partial-gravity data status (challenge text)
text: The challenge states there is currently no partial-gravity combustion data in PSI; data is expected later from LUCI and FM2. E-FIELD Flames mimicked partial gravity with an electric field; microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound intermediate gravity.

title: Highest oxygen tested in microgravity (challenge text)
text: The challenge states that the microgravity tests with the highest oxygen concentrations were ACME's Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G): the chamber held nitrogen and a flammable gas (e.g. propane) while an oxygen-nitrogen mixture of up to 85% oxygen flowed from a spherical burner, creating an inside-out flame.

title: Rockets and propellants are out of scope (challenge text)
text: The challenge states that fire safety involving rockets and propellants is generally beyond the scope of PSI research.
